claims.section: Power systems: network chain and high-voltage explanation
claims.knowledge: Generators, transformers, transmission, distribution and users form an electricity-delivery system. Raising voltage at fixed delivered power reduces current and resistive line heating.

claims.section: Power systems: slider, numerical readouts, graph and doubling-voltage answer
claims.knowledge: I=Pload/Vreceive; Ploss=I²R; Vsend=Vreceive+IR; Psend=Pload+Ploss. At fixed Pload and R, doubling receiving voltage quarters line loss.
claims.verification_and_scope: The last identities follow from series resistance and power balance. All selected values are illustrative. A resistive equivalent is used; reactive effects, generation losses and nonideal transformers are excluded.

claims.section: Energy accounting: units and conservation
claims.knowledge: Power is the rate of energy transfer; kWh measures energy. An energy budget includes delivered energy and all other destinations.
claims.verification_and_scope: No energy is destroyed by a loss: the word refers to energy unavailable in the intended useful output.

claims.section: Energy accounting: original numerical branches and destination captions
claims.knowledge: The course example allocates 300 kWh to 187 kWh thermal losses, 6 kWh plant use, 8 kWh network losses and 99 kWh delivered electricity.
claims.verification_and_scope: Exact figures and branch identities were checked against lecture slide 21. Plant use is separate from thermal and network losses. This is a particular thermal-generation example, not a modern fleet average.

claims.section: Energy accounting: scaled ribbon values and delivered percentage
claims.knowledge: The slider multiplies all four original branches by input/300; 99/300=33%. The four fractions always total one.
claims.verification_and_scope: Scaling is an explicit mathematical teaching assumption, not a plant performance model. Ribbon widths represent fractions; scaling total input changes labels while preserving fractions. Real efficiency need not remain fixed when load changes.

claims.section: Smart grid: measurements, resources and interoperability cards

claims.knowledge: Pgrid + Psolar + Pbattery = Pload. Positive battery power means discharge; negative means charge. Grid import is positive and export negative.
claims.verification_and_scope: An instantaneous, lossless conservation model with chosen sign conventions. Arrows show power direction; zero-power branches stop. Storage energy, elapsed time, state of charge, ratings, voltage and network constraints are not computed.

claims.section: Electric machines: section grouping
claims.knowledge: Motors convert electrical input to mechanical output; generators reverse the energy direction; transformers transfer electrical energy through changing magnetic flux.
claims.verification_and_scope: Umbrella mapping for the section. Individual motor, generator and transformer claims are M01–M06 and T01–T04.

claims.section: Machines: motor and generator energy directions

claims.knowledge: Opposite current directions on opposite coil sides experience forces that form a torque.

claims.knowledge: For N turns, magnetic moment is μ=NIA n; torque is τ=μ×B.

claims.verification_and_scope: Section 11.5 motor discussion. This statement concerns the simple commutated DC example, not all motor types.

claims.knowledge: For a planar coil in uniform B, flux per turn is Φ=BA cos θ, with θ measured from the field to the coil normal.
claims.verification_and_scope: Section 13.6, equation 13.16. The displayed per-turn flux differs from the N-turn flux linkage NΦ.

claims.section: Machines: generator EMF, speed slider and graph
claims.knowledge: A uniformly rotating N-turn coil has ε=NBAω sin θ, with ω=2πf. Doubling rotational frequency doubles the ideal EMF peak.
claims.verification_and_scope: Section 13.6, equations 13.17–13.18. Uniform field, fixed coil area, open-circuit ideal coil and constant speed are assumed. Displayed animation is slowed; no loaded-generator behavior is predicted.

claims.section: Transformer: shared-flux drawing
claims.knowledge: Alternating primary excitation establishes changing core flux linking two windings; energy transfers without a rotating shaft.
claims.verification_and_scope: Opening discussion and Figure 15.22. Both windings link the idealized common flux; geometry and drawn winding strokes are symbolic.

claims.section: Transformer: turns-ratio equation and voltage readouts
claims.knowledge: Vs/Vp=Ns/Np for an ideal transformer; the two electrical waveforms have the same frequency.
claims.verification_and_scope: Equations 15.20–15.21 derive both EMFs from the same changing flux. RMS values are used. Winding polarity is chosen consistently for the comparison.

claims.section: Transformer: current and power balance
claims.knowledge: For a lossless ideal transformer, VpIp=VsIs and Is/Ip=Np/Ns. Increasing voltage alone does not create power.
claims.verification_and_scope: Equation 15.22 and ideal power discussion. The interactive load is resistive and adjusted for each ratio to keep output power at 240 W.

claims.knowledge: The selected geared, full-converter chain is rotor → gearbox → generator → rectifier → DC link → inverter → transformer → grid.

claims.verification_and_scope: DOE describes the rotor-generator connection and geared/direct-drive alternatives. No numerical speed ratio, wind-speed curve or efficiency is claimed.

claims.knowledge: Rectification supplies a DC link, inversion supplies the AC grid side, and a transformer changes AC voltage for the connection.
claims.verification_and_scope: Functional explanations only. Practical conversion, filtering and grid-interface control details are omitted and not simulated.

models.title: Ideal square-wave H-bridge
models.parameters: Vdc: 12–96 V; default 48 V. Phase repeats over one electrical cycle.
assumptions: Purely resistive load; ideal switches; square-wave operation.
Q1 is upper left, Q2 lower left, Q3 upper right, Q4 lower right. Q1+Q4 is positive; Q3+Q2 is negative.
Same-leg pairs are never active together. Real gate timing and dead time are required but are not simulated.
Current-path dashes indicate conventional current direction, not electron speed.
checks: At phase 0.25 and 48 V, vout=+48 V. At phase 0.75, vout=−48 V.
The output is labeled square-wave AC, not sinusoidal filtered AC.

models.title: Ideal diode bridge
assumptions: Four ideal diodes; zero source impedance; resistive load; no smoothing capacitor.
Alternating diode pairs keep the same load polarity; output is pulsating DC.
A wire jump marks the AC/DC wire crossing with no connection.
checks: At phase 0.25, vin=48 V and vout=48 V. At phase 0.75, vin=−48 V and vout=48 V.
At zero crossings, vout=0 and no current path is highlighted.

models.title: Ideal averaged buck converter
models.formula: Vout,avg=D Vin; switch-node voltage is Vin during on-time and 0 during off-time.
models.parameters: Vin=48 V; duty ratio D=0.20–0.80, default 0.50.
assumptions: Periodic steady state, continuous inductor current and sufficiently large L and C.
The on-state connects input to the inductor; the off-state uses the freewheel diode.
Output is an averaged model; ripple, startup, discontinuous current and component sizing are not calculated.

models.title: Resistive-load AC voltage controller
models.formula: Let θ=2π phase and α be firing angle in radians. Pass Vpeak sin θ when θ mod π ≥ α; otherwise output 0. Vrms=(Vpeak/√2)√[1−α/π+sin(2α)/(2π)].
assumptions: Ideal antiparallel thyristors and purely resistive load; each conducting device turns off at current zero.
Same supply-cycle repetition; RMS control is not frequency conversion.
Only one example of the broader AC–AC category.
checks: At α=0°, Vrms≈33.941 V. At α=90°, Vrms=24 V.
Independent midpoint numerical integration at α=0°,30°,60°,90°,120°,150° agreed with the analytic RMS to better than 0.000001 V.

models.title: Resistive transmission equivalent
models.parameters: Pload=100 kW; total R=2 Ω; Vreceive=1–20 kV, default 10 kV.
assumptions: Single-phase, unity-power-factor resistive equivalent; voltage and current are RMS values. Transformers are ideal; reactive effects and generation losses are excluded.
Voltage is the receiving-end RMS voltage of the single-phase equivalent; the sending value includes the resistive drop.
At constant useful power and R, loss varies with the inverse square of receiving voltage.
checks: At 1 kV: I=100 A, Ploss=20 kW, Vsend=1.2 kV.
At 10 kV: I=10 A, Ploss=0.20 kW, Vsend=10.02 kV.
At 20 kV: I=5 A, Ploss=0.05 kW, Vsend=20.01 kV.
Vsend×I=Pload+Ploss for every displayed input.

models.title: Fixed-fraction course energy budget
assumptions: The original 300 kWh allocation comes from lecture slide 21.
Other slider inputs scale the same proportions; they are not measured operating data.
The 201/300 remainder comprises thermal losses, plant use and network losses; it is not all network loss.
checks: Delivered fraction: 99/300=0.33.

models.title: Instantaneous local power balance
models.parameters: Load=20–100 kW (default 60); solar=0–80 kW (default 35); battery=+20 kW discharge, 0 standby, or −20 kW charge.
assumptions: Lossless instantaneous balance, not an energy-duration simulation.
Positive grid power means import; negative means export.
No battery capacity, state of charge, inverter limits, voltage or network constraints.
checks: Default: grid=60−35−0=25 kW import.
Load 20, solar 80, battery +20: grid=−80 kW (export).
Load 100, solar 0, battery −20: grid=120 kW (import).

models.title: Instantaneous motor force diagram
models.parameters: Uniform B directed right; left current out of page and right current into page.
assumptions: Left conductor force points up and right force points down, giving clockwise torque.
This is an instantaneous cross section, with no angular-acceleration or performance model.
Commutation explanation applies to a simple DC motor.
checks: The two force arrows agree with the right-hand rule for I l×B.

models.title: Ideal rotating-coil generator
models.formula: Φ=BA cos θ per turn; ε=NBA(2πf) sin θ.
models.parameters: N=100; B=0.50 T; A=0.020 m²; f=0.5–2 Hz, default 1 Hz.
assumptions: Uniform field, planar coil, constant rotational frequency, open-circuit ideal EMF.
θ is the coil-normal-to-field angle, not the angle between the field and the coil plane.
Animation runs at one quarter of the stated physical cycle rate for inspection.
checks: At f=1 Hz, EMF peak=2π V≈6.283 V.
At θ=0°, flux per turn=0.010 Wb and EMF=0. At θ=90°, flux=0 and EMF is positive peak.
Doubling f doubles EMF peak; flux amplitude stays fixed.

models.title: Ideal transformer at constant power
models.formula: r=Ns/Np; Vs=r Vp; Ip=P/Vp; Is=P/Vs; Rload=Vs²/P.
assumptions: Ideal lossless transformer; both windings share common changing flux.
Load resistance changes with ratio to hold output power at 240 W.
No saturation, leakage, copper loss or core loss; winding strokes are symbolic.
Physical frequency is 60 Hz on both sides; flux animation is slowed to 0.3 Hz.
checks: Rload=15,60,240,540 Ω; VpIp=VsIs=240 W.
